hook.text: Ford knew the Pinto's fuel tank could explode in rear crashes. They calculated paying lawsuits was cheaper than a fix.

buildup.text: In the 1970s, Ford rushed the Pinto to market to compete with imports. Safety testing was cut short to meet deadlines.

discovery.text: Internal memos showed Ford estimated $11 per car to fix the defect but chose to pay expected death claims instead.

twist.text: When the memo leaked, outrage was massive. The cost-benefit analysis on human lives became a business ethics landmark.

climax.text: Ford recalled 1.5 million Pintos. The scandal showed cutting safety corners destroys trust faster than it saves.

punchline.text: Never put a price tag on safety. The cost of failure is trust.

quiz.question: Why did Ford initially not fix the Pinto fuel tank?
options: They calculated lawsuits would cost less

hook.text: In 1984, a Bhopal pesticide plant leaked toxic gas. Over 3,000 died overnight. Operations negligence killed a city.

buildup.text: Union Carbide's Bhopal plant had been cutting costs—reducing staff, skipping maintenance, and disabling safety systems.

discovery.text: Water entered a tank of methyl isocyanate, triggering a runaway reaction that released 40 tons of toxic gas.

twist.text: Every safety system that could have prevented the disaster had been shut down or was broken due to cost-cutting.

climax.text: Bhopal remains the world's worst industrial disaster. It led to global reforms in chemical plant safety regulations.

punchline.text: Cut safety costs and you pay with lives.

quiz.question: What caused the Bhopal disaster?
options: A design flaw in the product

hook.text: Two brand-new planes crashed within five months. 346 people died. Boeing's operations failures were systemic.

buildup.text: Boeing redesigned the 737 MAX with larger engines that changed flight characteristics. Software was added to compensate.

discovery.text: The MCAS software relied on a single sensor. When it failed, the system repeatedly pushed the nose down.

twist.text: Boeing pressured regulators, minimized pilot training, and hid the MCAS system's risks to speed certification.

climax.text: The MAX was grounded worldwide for nearly two years. Boeing lost $20 billion and its reputation for safety.

punchline.text: Speed-to-market killed people. Safety has no shortcut.

quiz.question: What software system caused the 737 MAX crashes?

hook.text: An oil rig explodes, killing 11 and spilling 4.9 million barrels into the Gulf. Operations failed at every level.

buildup.text: BP's Deepwater Horizon faced schedule pressure and cost overruns. Shortcuts were taken on safety tests and cement seals.

discovery.text: A cement barrier failed, gas surged up the well, and the blowout preventer—the last line of defense—didn't activate.

twist.text: Multiple warning signs were ignored in the hours before the explosion. Pressure test results were misread.

climax.text: The spill took 87 days to stop. BP paid $65 billion in cleanup, fines, and settlements. The Gulf suffered for years.

punchline.text: Ignoring warnings on the front line costs billions and lives.

quiz.question: What was the last line of defense that failed at Deepwater Horizon?

hook.text: A premium smartphone starts catching fire. Airlines ban it. Samsung recalls 2.5 million phones. Total cost: $5 billion.

buildup.text: Samsung rushed the Galaxy Note 7 to beat Apple's iPhone 7 launch. Battery testing was compressed.

discovery.text: The battery was too tightly packed, causing short circuits and thermal runaway. Both battery suppliers had defects.

twist.text: Samsung's first recall used batteries from a second supplier—which also had defects. The recall was recalled.

climax.text: The double recall was unprecedented. Samsung created an 8-point battery safety check and rebuilt its quality culture.

punchline.text: Rush the launch, recall the product, lose the billions.

quiz.question: Why did Samsung's first Note 7 recall fail?

hook.text: One ship stuck in a canal blocked $9.6 billion in trade per day for six days. One failure point froze global trade.

buildup.text: In March 2021, the Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal—a chokepoint handling 12% of global trade.

discovery.text: High winds and human error caused the grounding. The real failure was supply chain concentration through one canal.

twist.text: Over 400 ships queued on both sides. Ripple effects lasted months—container shortages, congestion, delayed deliveries.

climax.text: The incident exposed how fragile global trade is when it depends on a few geographic chokepoints.

punchline.text: One stuck ship showed the world how fragile global trade is.

quiz.question: What percentage of global trade passes through the Suez Canal?

hook.text: Floods in Thailand shut down 25% of the world's hard drive production. Computer prices spiked globally for months.

buildup.text: Thailand had become a global hub for hard drive manufacturing. Major suppliers concentrated in flood-prone areas.

discovery.text: When monsoon floods hit in 2011, entire industrial parks were submerged. Production stopped for months.

twist.text: Companies with diverse suppliers recovered quickly. Those dependent on Thai factories suffered massive revenue losses.

climax.text: The floods cost the global economy $45 billion and accelerated the shift from hard drives to solid-state storage.

punchline.text: Concentration is efficient until disaster hits that one spot.

quiz.question: What happened to hard drive prices after the 2011 Thai floods?

hook.text: In 2018, KFC closed 900 UK stores because it ran out of chicken. A chicken restaurant with no chicken.

buildup.text: KFC had just switched its UK logistics from Bidvest to DHL, a company with no experience in fresh food distribution.

discovery.text: DHL's single distribution center couldn't handle the volume. Deliveries failed within days of the switchover.

twist.text: KFC's cost-saving decision to consolidate from six warehouses to one created a single point of failure.

climax.text: KFC's cheeky apology ad rearranging its letters to FCK won public sympathy—but the logistics lesson was clear.

punchline.text: Saving on logistics cost KFC millions in lost chicken sales.

quiz.question: Why did KFC UK run out of chicken?
options: A logistics switch to one warehouse failed

hook.text: In 2021, automakers couldn't build cars over missing $1 chips. A tiny component halted billion-dollar production lines.

buildup.text: When COVID hit, automakers cancelled chip orders. Chip makers shifted capacity to consumer electronics.

discovery.text: When car demand rebounded, automakers found they'd lost their place in the queue. Lead times stretched to a year.

twist.text: A $1 chip shortage in a $40,000 car shows how one missing component can stop an entire product.

climax.text: The shortage cost the auto industry $210 billion in 2021 alone and triggered reshoring investments in chip fabrication.

punchline.text: Cancel your chip order today. Lose your car production for a year.

quiz.question: Why did automakers face a chip shortage in 2021?
options: They cancelled orders during COVID then couldn't get back in the queue

hook.text: A 10-minute fire at a Philips chip plant cost Ericsson $400 million. Nokia, using the same plant, lost nothing.

buildup.text: In 2000, lightning struck a Philips semiconductor plant in New Mexico. A small fire contaminated millions of chips.

discovery.text: Both Ericsson and Nokia sourced radio frequency chips from that plant. Philips told both the delay would be short.

twist.text: Nokia escalated fast—sourcing chips from Japan and redesigning alternatives. Ericsson waited and trusted Philips.

climax.text: Nokia barely missed a beat. Ericsson couldn't make phones for months and exited the handset business two years later.

punchline.text: Same disaster. Different responses. Opposite outcomes.

quiz.question: Why did Nokia survive the Philips fire while Ericsson didn't?

hook.text: An airbag meant to save your life fires metal shrapnel at you. Takata's defective airbags killed 27 people worldwide.

buildup.text: Takata used ammonium nitrate as a propellant—it was cheaper but degraded in heat and humidity over time.

discovery.text: The propellant became unstable and caused inflators to rupture violently instead of deploying the airbag safely.

twist.text: Takata knew about the defect for years but concealed test data and resisted recalls to protect its business.

climax.text: The recall covered 67 million vehicles—the largest automotive recall in history. Takata went bankrupt in 2017.

punchline.text: Covering up a defect cost more than fixing it ever would have.

quiz.question: Why did Takata's airbag inflators fail?
options: The propellant degraded in heat and humidity

hook.text: A radiation machine gave patients 100x the intended dose. Software bugs killed people. No one tested properly.

buildup.text: The Therac-25 was a computer-controlled radiation machine used in hospitals in the 1980s.

discovery.text: A race condition in the software allowed the machine to fire a high-energy beam without the required safety shield.

twist.text: The manufacturer blamed operators, not software. Patients and staff reported problems but were dismissed for months.

climax.text: Six patients were overdosed, three fatally. The case became the landmark study in software safety engineering.

punchline.text: Software can kill. Test it like lives depend on it.

quiz.question: What caused the Therac-25 overdoses?

hook.text: In 1982, seven people in Chicago died from cyanide-laced Tylenol. J&J's response became a masterclass in crisis ops.

buildup.text: Someone had tampered with Tylenol bottles on store shelves—inserting cyanide into capsules and returning them.

discovery.text: J&J immediately recalled 31 million bottles nationwide—even though the tampering was limited to one city.

twist.text: The recall cost $100 million. Analysts predicted Tylenol was dead. But J&J's swift action rebuilt trust.

climax.text: J&J invented the tamper-proof seal, relaunched Tylenol in new packaging, and regained market share within a year.

punchline.text: Act fast. Protect people first. Trust returns.

quiz.question: How did J&J respond to the Tylenol tampering?

hook.text: VW programmed cars to cheat emissions tests. They passed in the lab and polluted 40 times the limit on the road.

buildup.text: VW's diesel engines couldn't meet US emissions standards and still deliver the promised performance.

discovery.text: Engineers installed defeat devices—software that detected test conditions and reduced emissions only during testing.

twist.text: The cheat affected 11 million vehicles worldwide. An operations culture of pressure and fear enabled the fraud.

climax.text: VW paid over $30 billion in fines and settlements. The CEO resigned and multiple executives faced criminal charges.

punchline.text: Cheating the test doesn't fix the problem. It multiplies it.

quiz.question: What did VW's defeat device do?

hook.text: NASA lost a $125 million spacecraft because one team used metric and another imperial. A unit conversion error.

buildup.text: The Mars Climate Orbiter launched in 1998 to study the Martian atmosphere from orbit.

discovery.text: Lockheed Martin sent thruster data in pound-seconds. NASA's software expected newton-seconds. Nobody checked.

twist.text: The orbiter flew too close to Mars and burned up in the atmosphere. A simple handoff error destroyed the mission.

climax.text: NASA reformed its verification processes and made unit-checking mandatory across all contractor interfaces.

punchline.text: A $125 million lesson: always check the units.

quiz.question: What caused the Mars Climate Orbiter failure?

hook.text: Christmas 2013: FedEx and UPS failed to deliver millions of packages on time. Presents arrived after the holiday.

buildup.text: Online shopping surged beyond forecasts. Last-minute orders overwhelmed sorting hubs and delivery networks.

discovery.text: Carriers had capacity for projected volumes but not the actual spike. Forecasting missed e-commerce's acceleration.

twist.text: Retailers had promised delivery dates they couldn't control—the carrier's failure became the retailer's broken promise.

climax.text: After 2013, carriers invested billions in automation and surge capacity. Amazon began building its own delivery network.

punchline.text: Promise a date, own the delivery—or someone else will.

quiz.question: What caused the 2013 holiday delivery failure?
options: Online shopping surged beyond capacity forecasts

hook.text: Hershey launched a new ERP system before Halloween. Orders couldn't ship. $100 million in candy sat in warehouses.

buildup.text: In 1999, Hershey went live with SAP, Siebel, and Manugistics simultaneously—a massive IT and logistics overhaul.

discovery.text: The systems couldn't communicate properly. Orders entered the system but couldn't be processed, picked, or shipped.

twist.text: Hershey launched right before its peak season—Halloween and Christmas—when flawless execution mattered most.

climax.text: Hershey's revenue dropped 12% that quarter. Competitors grabbed shelf space that took years to recover.

punchline.text: Never launch a new system during your busiest season.

quiz.question: When did Hershey launch its new ERP system?

hook.text: Target opened 124 stores in Canada and closed them all within two years. Logistics failures doomed the expansion.

buildup.text: Target entered Canada in 2013, opening stores at a pace that overwhelmed its supply chain and distribution systems.

discovery.text: Product data was riddled with errors—wrong dimensions, wrong costs. Shelves were empty or filled with the wrong items.

twist.text: Canadians expected Target's US experience. They got empty shelves and higher prices. The brand promise was broken.

climax.text: Target lost $7 billion and exited Canada entirely. The failure was rooted in bad data and rushed logistics.

punchline.text: Bad data plus rushed execution equals billion-dollar failure.

quiz.question: What caused Target Canada's failure?
options: Bad product data and rushed logistics

hook.text: Boeing's 787 Dreamliner was grounded worldwide after lithium-ion batteries caught fire. The entire fleet sat idle.

buildup.text: Boeing outsourced 70% of the Dreamliner's production to global suppliers to reduce costs and speed development.

discovery.text: Parts arrived late, didn't fit, or had quality issues. The battery was sourced through a chain Boeing barely supervised.

twist.text: Over-outsourcing meant Boeing lost visibility and control. When the battery failed, finding the root cause took months.

climax.text: The Dreamliner was delivered 3 years late and billions over budget. Boeing vowed to bring more production in-house.

punchline.text: Outsource the work but not the responsibility.

quiz.question: What caused the Dreamliner's battery problems?
options: A deeply outsourced supply chain with little oversight

hook.text: Nike's demand planning software miscalculated. Too many slow sellers, not enough best sellers. Cost: $100 million.

buildup.text: In 2001, Nike deployed i2's demand planning software to forecast what shoes to produce and in what quantities.

discovery.text: The software generated wildly wrong forecasts—overestimating unpopular shoes and underestimating popular ones.

twist.text: Nike blamed the software. i2 blamed the implementation. The real failure was deploying without proper testing.

climax.text: Nike lost $100 million in sales, its stock dropped 20%, and the CEO acknowledged the technology fumble publicly.

punchline.text: Bad software forecasts make expensive shoes nobody buys.

quiz.question: What went wrong with Nike's demand planning software?

hook.text: The US government launched Healthcare.gov in 2013. On day one, only 6 people successfully enrolled. Six.

buildup.text: The website was supposed to serve millions of Americans signing up for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act.

discovery.text: The site crashed under load. It was built by 55 contractors with no single integrator and no end-to-end testing.

twist.text: Warning signs appeared months before launch. Officials ignored them and insisted on the October 1 deadline.

climax.text: A rescue team from Silicon Valley rebuilt critical systems in weeks. The site stabilized by December.

punchline.text: 55 contractors, no testing, one deadline. Recipe for failure.

quiz.question: How many people enrolled on Healthcare.gov's first day?

hook.text: Denver International Airport delayed opening 16 months because of an automated baggage system that shredded luggage.

buildup.text: The airport planned a fully automated underground baggage system—26 miles of track and 4,000 telecars.

discovery.text: The system was wildly complex. Bags flew off carts, jammed at intersections, and were destroyed by the machinery.

twist.text: Engineers warned it was too ambitious. But the project was too far along to stop—sunk cost fallacy in action.

climax.text: The delay cost $500 million. The automated system was eventually scrapped entirely in favor of a simple conveyor system.

punchline.text: $500 million for a system that was replaced by conveyor belts.

quiz.question: What happened to Denver Airport's automated baggage system?
options: It was scrapped and replaced with conveyors
It was sold to another airport

hook.text: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975. Then buried it to protect film profits. By 2012, Kodak was bankrupt.

buildup.text: Kodak dominated photography for a century. Film, chemicals, and paper were a massively profitable operations machine.

discovery.text: Kodak's operations were optimized for film. Every factory, supply chain, and process assumed film would last forever.

twist.text: When digital cameras took over, Kodak's entire operations infrastructure became obsolete overnight.

climax.text: Kodak's failure wasn't ignorance—they invented digital. It was an operations strategy locked to the wrong product.

punchline.text: Optimizing for yesterday's product guarantees tomorrow's bankruptcy.

quiz.question: When did Kodak invent the digital camera?

hook.text: Airbus built the A380 in factories across Europe. The wiring harnesses didn't fit. Two years of delays followed.

buildup.text: The A380's sections were built in France, Germany, Spain, and the UK, then assembled in Toulouse.

discovery.text: German and French teams used different versions of design software. Their wiring bundles were literally incompatible.

twist.text: 530 kilometers of wiring per plane had to be partially rerouted by hand. Each plane needed weeks of rework.

climax.text: The delays cost Airbus $6 billion and the CEO resigned. It was a failure of cross-site coordination, not engineering.

punchline.text: Different software versions, incompatible wiring, $6 billion.

quiz.question: What caused the A380 wiring disaster?
options: Teams used different design software versions

hook.text: The unsinkable ship sank on its maiden voyage. 1,500 people died because operations planners believed their own hype.

buildup.text: Titanic was an engineering marvel with a fatal operational flaw: not enough lifeboats for all passengers.

discovery.text: Regulations were outdated. Titanic exceeded the tonnage threshold but carried lifeboats for only a third of capacity.

twist.text: Officers received iceberg warnings but maintained full speed—pressure to arrive on time overrode caution.

climax.text: After the disaster, maritime regulations were rewritten: enough lifeboats for everyone and 24/7 radio watch.

punchline.text: Hubris sinks ships. Humility saves lives.

quiz.question: Why didn't Titanic have enough lifeboats?
options: They fell off in a storm
Regulations were outdated for its size

hook.text: Apollo 13's main oxygen tank exploded in space. Redundant systems kept three astronauts alive for four days.

buildup.text: Redundancy means having backup systems, suppliers, or capacity that activate when the primary fails.

discovery.text: It costs more upfront but prevents catastrophic single-point failures that can destroy operations entirely.

twist.text: Lean thinking sometimes eliminates redundancy as waste. But critical systems need backup—lean doesn't mean fragile.

climax.text: The best operations balance efficiency with resilience—lean where possible, redundant where failure is unacceptable.

punchline.text: Backup plans feel wasteful—until you need them.

quiz.question: Why is redundancy important in operations?

hook.text: Boeing had the best engineers. VW had the best cars. Both failed because their cultures tolerated shortcuts.

buildup.text: Operations failures trace back to culture—pressure to hit targets, fear of speaking up, and tolerance of risk.

discovery.text: A culture that punishes bad news ensures bad news is hidden—until it becomes a catastrophe.

twist.text: Every post-mortem of major failures finds warning signs that were ignored, dismissed, or suppressed.

climax.text: Organizations that celebrate problem-finding over problem-hiding catch failures early when fixes are cheap.

punchline.text: A culture of silence is a culture of risk.

quiz.question: What does a culture that punishes bad news produce?

hook.text: Healthcare.gov, Hershey's ERP, Denver's baggage system—all launched without proper testing. All failed spectacularly.

buildup.text: Testing reveals what will break before customers experience it. Skipping it saves weeks but costs years.

discovery.text: End-to-end testing, stress testing, and user acceptance testing each catch different categories of failure.

twist.text: The pressure to meet a launch date is the most common reason testing gets cut. Deadlines kill quality.

climax.text: Companies that delay launches to complete testing almost always outperform those that launch broken and patch later.

punchline.text: Launch late with quality. Never launch broken.

quiz.question: Why is testing most often skipped?
options: It's not needed for simple systems

hook.text: Nokia asked Philips tough questions right away. Ericsson waited. Transparency separates survival from failure.

buildup.text: Early warning systems detect problems when they're small and fixable—before they cascade into full failures.

discovery.text: Transparency across supply chain partners, departments, and levels enables faster response to emerging risks.

twist.text: Most organizations have the data to detect problems early. They lack the culture to act on weak signals.

climax.text: Companies sharing real-time data with partners and empowering workers to escalate recover from any disruption.

punchline.text: See the signal early. Act immediately. Survive.

quiz.question: What enables early warning in operations?

hook.text: Every operations disaster in this course shares one root cause: someone decided a shortcut was worth the risk.

buildup.text: Shortcuts save money in the short term: less testing, fewer suppliers, cheaper materials, faster timelines.

discovery.text: But the hidden costs compound: recalls, lawsuits, lost customers, destroyed reputations, and sometimes lost lives.

twist.text: Companies that survived invested heavily in prevention afterward—paying more than the shortcut ever saved.

climax.text: The lesson is universal: invest in quality, safety, and resilience upfront. Failure always costs more than prevention.

punchline.text: Shortcuts are the most expensive path in operations.

quiz.question: What do all major operations failures have in common?
options: Someone took a shortcut they shouldn't have
